measurement, on the base checkpoint, is void. None of it is evidence about
the model. It only shows the measuring setup drifted from the earlier run
it was calibrated against.

The numbers below were still computed and saved. They are worth reporting
for what they show. Every one of them carries that same void label.

All three widths beat pure chance, on the base checkpoint. The observed
wave strength ranked first out of 200 random-shuffle comparisons, at every
one of the three widths tested.

On the base checkpoint, the 140-character width gave a wave length of 70
characters. The 200-character width gave 100 characters, and the
280-character width gave 140 characters. Each is exactly half of its own
width.

The longest and shortest of those lengths differ by 70 characters. That is
more than the 10-character difference allowed for calling them one fixed
length. All three lengths sit at exactly half their own width. On that same base
checkpoint, that is a matching ratio of 0.5 in every case. So the headline
call, on the base checkpoint, is that the wave's length grows with the
width. That call is
void, for the reason above.

At the 140-character width, the sub-word-piece control could not even be
computed. No held-out test text reached the sub-word position the
comparison needed. At the 200-character width, the two ways of counting
position gave wave lengths 15.277055 characters apart, on the base
checkpoint. At the 280-character width, they gave wave lengths 17.735970
characters apart, on the base checkpoint. Both gaps pass the 3-character
cutoff for treating the two as the same wave. So the wave at those two
widths is credited to counting characters, not to counting sub-word pieces.

The escape-hatch check looked past character 150 into a line, on the base
checkpoint. Both far ends tested were represented there: positions 211
through 245, and positions 246 through 280. So the void above is not
explained away as nothing being measurable that far into a line.

## Does this match what was expected

No, on more than one count. This section says so plainly rather than
smoothing it over.

Before the run, the recorded concern was that the sanity check would most
likely fail low. Three past readings of this exact 140-character-only
measurement, on the base checkpoint, were 0.700601, 0.549000, and 0.664024.
All three, on that same base checkpoint, sat below the allowed range's low
end of 0.767394. The check instead failed high, on the base checkpoint, at
0.859740. That is the opposite direction from the one anticipated.

An earlier, closely related run, on the base checkpoint, had found this
same kind of wave needing only 1 direction. On that same base checkpoint,
that single direction carried 95.3 percent of the wave's shape. This run
instead needed 93 to 196 directions, on the same base checkpoint, across
its three widths, to reach that same 95 percent mark.
That is a large, unexplained change in the wave's basic shape between the
two runs.

Because the required sanity check failed, this run's outcome is neither of
the two rival ideas it set out to test. It is not "the wave has one fixed
length." It is not "the wave's length is an artifact of the width" either.
It is a third outcome, on the base checkpoint: the run cannot be read as
evidence for or against either idea. Every wave number above is exploratory
only, kept for the record. None of it is usable as a finding about the
model.

## What in these files does not fit

These are open questions raised about this run. A few more that this review
turned up on its own follow them.

**The wave's length always came out to exactly half the width tested.**
Counting by character or by sub-word piece made no difference. At every
width tried (140, 200, and 280 characters), the found wave completed
exactly 2 full cycles across the tested span, with no exception. A method
that always reports two cycles, regardless of width or counting scheme, may
be producing that number itself. It may not be detecting it in the network.

**The sanity check failed on the wrong side.** Going in, every recorded
warning pointed toward a low failure. That warning rested on three past
readings of the same measurement. The check instead failed high. Whatever
reasoning predicted trouble was reasoning about the wrong direction. That
weakens confidence in the rest of that reasoning.

**Five reruns meant to measure this run's own natural variation all landed
on the identical choice.** Five reruns, each holding out a different six
documents, were meant to show how much the sanity check's result would
normally wander. All five picked the identical internal point and the
identical readout strength. The resulting allowed range came out narrower
than a limit the project had set for itself in advance. That limit exists
precisely to flag this kind of trouble. The flag was raised in the record,
but it changed no decision.

**Line-by-line records survive for only three of the nine line widths.**
Those nine widths fed the single most important choice of this whole run:
which internal point to search for a wave. The saved line-by-line detail
behind that choice exists for only three of those nine widths. The other
six widths' line-by-line detail was not kept anywhere in this run's saved
files. That choice cannot be independently checked line by line. Only its
already-summed totals can be trusted or questioned.

**The number of directions needed for this signal jumped by roughly one
hundred times.** A closely related earlier run, on the base checkpoint,
needed only 1 direction to carry 95.3 percent of this same kind of signal.
This run needed 93 to 196 directions for that same 95 percent mark, on the
base checkpoint, across its three widths. Whatever theory expected a
narrow, one-direction signal does not obviously fit a signal this much
wider.

**The wave was detectable, then not, then detectable again, as line
position grew.** The widest test texts were split into eight bands of line
position. The wave was found beyond chance for positions 211 through 245.
It was absent for positions 176 through 210. It was found again beyond
chance for positions 246 through 280. A story where the wave simply fades
out with distance does not fit a gap that closes back up further out.

content.text: Decisive: this run reproduces seed D2's instrument to 6–9 significant figures on independently written code. Writing my reading of record.

input.command:
cat > out/OPERATOR_READING_seedC1.md <<'EOF'
# Operating session's reading of record, seed C1

The pipeline's own write-up is `TAKEAWAYS_seedC1.md`, produced by the write stage
and passed through both language gates untouched. This file is separate on
purpose: it is the operating session's reading, and it corrects one thing the
write stage got wrong about the run's own records. It changes no measured number
and no decision.

## 1. The answer to the research question

The question asked: at probe windows of 140, 200 and 280 characters, where a
periodicity clears its shuffle null, is its wavelength INVARIANT in characters or
PROPORTIONAL to the window?

**The run is void, and the question is not answered.** The anchor gate failed, and
the question's own rule says an out-of-band anchor voids every ripple result as an
instrument fault, not as evidence about the model. That rule was written before the
run and is not being softened now.

For the record, the void numbers point at PROPORTIONAL, and they do so about as
hard as numbers can. All three windows cleared their null at rank 1 of 200. The
wavelengths were 70, 100 and 140 characters at windows 140, 200 and 280. Every one
is exactly half its own window. The wavelength-to-window ratio is 0.5 three times
over, so the ratio gap is exactly 0. None of this is admissible.

## 2. Why the anchor failed, and why "the instrument drifted" is the wrong reading

The anchor statistic came out at 0.859740 against a band of 0.767394 to 0.794606.
It failed high, not low. The write stage read that as the measuring setup having
drifted from the run it was calibrated against. The run's own records rule that
reading out.

This run reproduces the previous asking's instrument almost exactly, on code an
agent wrote from scratch without seeing that previous run:

| quantity | seed D2, committed 2026-08-21 | seed C1, this run |
|---|---|---|
| best readout, held-out, pooled over nine widths | 5 | 5 |
| held-out fit there, pooled over nine widths | 0.657823 | 0.657823 |
| held-out fit there, width 140 alone | 0.549167 | 0.549167 |
| ridge strength | 1000 | 1000 |
| held-out positions, all nine widths | 99692 | 99692 |
| range-check bins at or below label 140 | -24.343564, -35.165575, -18.826312, -3.827423 | -24.343593, -35.165610, -18.826348, -3.827435 |
| range-check bins above label 175 | -39.367425, -90.250193, -146.593113 | -39.367383, -90.250139, -146.593033 |

Nine numbers, two independent implementations, agreeing to between five and nine
significant figures. The residual difference is the size expected from storing
activations at reduced precision. An instrument that drifted would not do this.

What actually happened is a construct mismatch, and the run's own
recorded-never-gated readings show it directly. Four different fits all get called
"held-out fit at width 140" in this project's history, and they are not the same
quantity:

| what is fitted, and where the layer comes from | scored at width 140 | source |
|---|---|---|
| ridge on train pooled over nine widths, layer chosen on held-out pooled over nine widths | 0.549167 | seed D2, and this run |
| the same probe at seed D2's calibration-preferred layer | 0.700601 | seed D2 |
| ridge on train pooled over widths 20 to 140, layer 6 | 0.664024 | seed D2.1 |
| ridge on train at width 140 alone, layer chosen on train at width 140 alone | **0.859740** | this run, first measurement of this construct |

The band's centre, 0.781, is a fifth quantity again: a fit pooled over the widths
20 to 140 and scored pooled over those same widths (0.780903 in seed D1, 0.781031
in seed D2.1). This run measured its own version of that, 0.612773, but with the
nine-width probe, which is a sixth thing.

So the anchor gate compared a statistic that had never been measured before against
a band centred on a different statistic. The gate did its job; the centre was wrong
for the quantity it was gating.

The gate commit's answer A6 chose the reading that produced 0.859740, and the
pre-run grounding note (gate commit B1) predicted the run would void from below,
citing 0.700601, 0.549 and 0.664024. That prediction was wrong in direction, and it
was wrong for an instructive reason: a probe fitted and selected at one wrap width
alone is a *better* probe at that width than any probe that has to serve nine
widths at once. Specialising the fit raised the number; it did not lower it.

## 3. The dispersion rule worked, and its own narrow-band flag fired

The five resplits gave 0.867072, 0.876217, 0.866433, 0.861897 and 0.860696. Their
median is 0.866433 and their unscaled median absolute deviation is 0.004535, giving
a half-width of 0.013606. The measured spread was not zero, so
`WRONG_VARIANCE_SOURCE` correctly did not fire; the five held-out document sets
differ, and their fit qualities differ with them.

All five resplits independently chose the same readout (7) and the same ridge
strength (100). That is a stability result about the selection, not a zero-variance
error.

The run's own `band_half_width_below_0.02` flag came out true, which the gate
commit required to be quoted whenever the anchor fails. Quoting it: the band was
0.0136 wide either side, and the anchor statistic sits 4.8 median-absolute-
deviations above the band's centre while sitting only 1.5 of them from the median
of the resplits that measured the spread. Read plainly: the statistic is highly
reproducible and the centre is in the wrong place.

## 4. The finding that matters most, even though it is void

Every one of the five computable periodicity readouts, at three windows and under
two labellings, put its maximum power at exactly **two cycles across the profile**.
Not at the same wavelength. At the same cycle count.

- window 140, characters: 2 cycles, 70 characters, rank 1 of 200
- window 200, characters: 2 cycles, 100 characters, rank 1 of 200
- window 280, characters: 2 cycles, 140 characters, rank 1 of 200
- window 200, tokens: 2 cycles, 33.5 tokens, rank 1 of 200
- window 280, tokens: 2 cycles, 45.5 tokens, rank 1 of 200

The saved similarity profile says why. At window 140 it runs 0.1814 at distance 1,
falls steadily to -0.1103 at distance 100, then turns and rises to 0.1622 at
distance 140. That is one smooth arc, not a wave. A degree-2 polynomial cannot
absorb an arc of that shape, and what it leaves behind has its power at the lowest
few cycle counts: 6.03e-05 at one cycle, 8.84e-05 at two, 7.03e-05 at three. Two
cycles wins by a nose over its own neighbours.

The shuffle null cannot catch this. Shuffling labels within a document destroys all
structure, so a null profile is flat, and *any* smooth non-polynomial shape beats
all 200 draws. The test as written asks "is there structure here that a parabola
does not explain", not "is there a periodicity here". Those are different
questions, and a decaying similarity curve answers yes to the first while having no
wave in it at all.

Two consequences follow, and both are about the design rather than the model.

First, the invariance fork cannot separate its two horns with this statistic. A
fixed cycle count is proportional to the window by construction, so PROPORTIONAL is
what this readout returns whenever the profile is a smooth arc. The fork's
"artifact of the probe window" horn is exactly right here, and it is right about
the readout, not about the model.

Second, the token-position control cannot do its job either. Both labellings landed
on two cycles. The control converts the token period to characters and asks whether
the two differ by more than 3 characters. Two cycles in token units and two cycles
in character units convert to different character numbers whenever the profile
lengths differ, so the control credits characters (gaps of 15.28 and 17.74
characters) while both labellings are showing the same artifact. The control
measures a unit conversion, not a distinction.

## 5. Two premises of the question did not hold

The question's reasoning rests on seed D1's measured ambient dimension of 1, with
the first component carrying 95.3 percent. This run measured 93, 141 and 196
directions to reach 95 percent, at windows 140, 200 and 280, on centred per-label
mean vectors at readout 5. The first component carries 0.437, 0.305 and 0.200.
Whatever seed D1 measured, it is not the same object as this, and the "spacing
equals the window divided by one" argument that motivated the three-aperture design
does not survive contact with 93 to 196 directions.

The represented-range escape hatch also did not behave as its two-sided rule
imagined. Bins are represented, then not, then represented again as the label grows:
1-35, 36-70, 71-105 and 106-140 represented; 141-175 (excluded by rule) not;
176-210 not; 211-245 and 246-280 represented. The rule's decision,
ABOVE_150_REPRESENTED, is correct as written and closes the escape hatch. But a
pattern that switches off and back on is not the "signal fades with distance"
picture the hatch was built around.

## 6. What a next asking would have to change

This is a recommendation, not a result. The question's own rule says a failed
anchor blocks any next seed, so nothing below is licensed until the anchor is
re-specified.

1. The anchor's band centre must come from the same construct as its statistic.
   Either centre the band on a number measured with the anchor's own procedure, or
   define the anchor as the construct 0.781 came from. Mixing them is what voided
   this run, and it has now voided two askings in a row for two different reasons.
2. The periodicity statistic needs a null that keeps the smooth part and destroys
   only the periodic part. A within-document label shuffle destroys everything, so
   it cannot tell an arc from a wave. A phase-randomised or trend-preserving
   surrogate would put the two on the same footing.
3. A readout whose answer is a fixed cycle count cannot decide a fork between
   "fixed in characters" and "proportional to the window". Either the statistic must
   be reported in absolute units with the cycle count free, or the fork needs a
   different discriminator.
4. The probe pooled over all nine wrap widths is a poor probe: it scores -7.99 at
   width 20 and -1.18 at width 40. Every downstream number, the represented-range
   bins included, inherits that. Pooling only over widths that share a label range
   is the change seed D2.1 already made, and dropping it here cost accuracy.
EOF

content.text:
Done. All modes ran in order; both boxes confirmed torn down via the API; $0.69 of the $15 cap; 67 artifacts, 19 MB, all under `out/`.

## The answer

**The question is not answered. The run is void, by its own pre-registered rule.**

The anchor gate measured **0.859740** against a measured band of **[0.767394, 0.794606]** (centre 0.781, half-width 3×MAD = 0.013606 from five resplits). Outside the band ⇒ instrument fault ⇒ every ripple number is not evidence about the model. I did not move the centre.

It failed **high**, not low. The pre-run grounding reader predicted a low failure, citing 0.700601 / 0.549 / 0.664024. Wrong direction.

## Why "the instrument drifted" is the wrong reading

This run, on code written from scratch by a claim-blind agent, reproduces seed D2's instrument:

| | seed D2 (2026-08-21) | seed C1 |
|---|---|---|
| best readout | 5 | 5 |
| held-out fit, nine widths | 0.657823 | **0.657823** |
| held-out fit, width 140 | 0.549167 | **0.549167** |
| held-out positions | 99692 | **99692** |
| 7 range-check bins | −24.343564 … −146.593113 | −24.343593 … −146.593033 |

Nine numbers, five to nine significant figures, two implementations. The instrument is sound. What failed is a **construct mismatch**: five different fits in this project's history are all called "held-out fit at width 140", and the band's centre (0.781, a fit pooled over widths 20–140) is not the anchor's statistic (fit *and* layer-selected at width 140 alone — measured for the first time here, at 0.8597). Specialising the probe to one width makes it *better*, which is why it overshot. The statistic sits 17.4 MADs above the centre but only 1.5 MADs from the median of the resplits that measured the spread.

## The finding that matters most, though it is void

All five computable readouts — three windows × characters, two × tokens — put maximum power at **exactly two cycles across the profile**. Not the same wavelength; the same cycle count. Wavelengths 70 / 100 / 140 = exactly half of 140 / 200 / 280; ratio gap exactly 0.

The saved profile shows why: at window 140 it runs 0.1814 at distance 1, down to −0.1103 at distance 100, back up to 0.1622 at 140. One smooth arc, not a wave. Degree-2 detrending can't absorb it, leaving power at the lowest cycles (1 cycle 6.03e−05, 2 cycles 8.84e−05, 3 cycles 7.03e−05). The within-document shuffle null flattens *everything*, so any smooth non-polynomial shape ranks 1 of 200. The statistic asks "is there structure a parabola misses", not "is there a periodicity".

Consequences for the design, not the model: a fixed cycle count is proportional to the window **by construction**, so this readout returns PROPORTIONAL whenever the profile is an arc — the fork can't separate its horns. And the token control credits characters (gaps 15.28 / 17.74 chars) purely because two cycles converts differently in two unit systems; it measures a unit conversion, not a distinction.

Two premises also failed: ambient dimension came out **93 / 141 / 196**, not seed D1's 1 (first component 0.44 / 0.31 / 0.20, not 0.953) — which dissolves the "spacing equals window ÷ 1" argument the three-aperture design rests on. And the represented-range check went represented → not → represented as labels grow (escape hatch correctly closed: `ABOVE_150_REPRESENTED`).

## Deliverables

- `out/TAKEAWAYS_seedC1.md` — pipeline's write stage, untouched; both gates re-run by me: 0 codes/2392 words, 0 unscoped sentences.
- `out/OPERATOR_READING_seedC1.md` — my reading, incl. the correction above (the write stage called the failure instrument drift).
- `out/GATE_COMMIT_seedC1.md` (15/15 answered), `out/seedC1_design_diff_triage.json`, `out/seedC1_post_elicit_triage.json` (8 elicited questions, top 3 all grounded "reproduces").
- `out/DEVIATIONS_seedC1.md` — 4 booked, incl. the one real defect I fixed: an operator-precedence typo (`work_dir / "x%d.npz" % n`) in the built runner that the stdlib-only self-test structurally could not reach.
- `out/results_seedC1/` (19 records, full null spectra, per-label mean vectors, per-row files), `out/results_seedC1_launch1_failed/`, both per-launch launcher copies.

Nothing frozen was edited — `pipeline.js`, `triage_workflow.js`, `gates/`, `frozen/` all still at their original mtimes.

One caveat on the triage output: the skeptic fan-out uses an ablation-oriented default confound menu, so several cruxes reason about "off-distribution ablation" in a run that performs no intervention. Those are noise; the three groundings and the elicited questions are the load-bearing part.
